newsitem.title: TAJIKISTAN: Distrust, armed bands threaten Tajik peace.
newsitem.headline: Distrust, armed bands threaten Tajik peace.

text.p: The Tajik government and its armed Islamist opposition foe were confident on Tuesday that a deal to end four years of civil war in the ex-Soviet republic would be signed in Moscow on Friday.
The conflict has claimed the lives of tens of thousands in this Central Asian state, which borders Afghanistan and China among the remote Pamir mountains, known locally as "the roof of the world".

But diplomats say peace is threatened by distrust sparked by the imminent return of opposition guerrillas to the capital Dushanbe and a collapse in law and order in the impoverished country of six million.
"It's time to sign," Zafar Saidov, Tajik President Imomali Rakhmonov's spokesman, said in Dushanbe.

Davlat Usmon, commander of the Tajik opposition's armed forces, told Reuters: "I look at this agreement optimistically. All questions on the establishment of peace are decided, only a few technical questions remain."
The optimism is based on a ceasefire agreed last December brokered by Iran, Russia and the United Nations. Earlier ceasefires often collapsed as soon as they were signed.

"There's been an amazing change in the last seven months, we have an effective ceasefire which makes a huge difference on the ground," said Milos Strugar, a political officer with the U.N.'s small military observer team in Tajikistan.
"You see fighters coming back to their villages and getting married and working their land again," he said. "It has had an important psychological effect on fighters on both sides."

But the opposition delegation travelling to Moscow is angry over a stalled prisoner exchange and is haggling with Rakhmonov over which of the 30 percent of government posts should go to the opposition under a power sharing arrangement.
"The agreements aren't that clear, they aren't that precise," said a western diplomat on condition of anonymity.

Even if the government and opposition do sign an accord in the Kremlin on Friday -- to be witnessed by Russian President Boris Yeltsin -- maverick armed bands and hardliners inside both camps make for an extremely fragile peace.
"There are people on both sides who want to make it work," said the diplomat, "but they've got their work cut out for them."
The return of 460 armed opposition guerrillas to Dushanbe, who are supposed to be integrated with government troops into a new national force, is the main cause of alarm.

Diplomats said a aggressive government commander from the south, who earlier this year slammed negotiations with the opposition and who led a mutiny in 1996, moved his armour towards the capital last week.

The government itself is unhappy about such a sizeable opposition force inside the capital. "We are against this in principle," Saidov said. "But Mr Rakhmonov has gone all the way to meet the opposition and compromise."
The foundations of any real peace are Rakhmonov's and the opposition's ability to settle differences and govern.
Tajikistan is faced with the return of thousands of refugees, it feels menacing shockwaves from fighting in neighbouring Afghanistan and its inflation-hit economy is in a nosedive.
"The main threat to the stability of this country is the extremely tough economic situation, the poverty," Strugar said.
